title: Discipline
intro: The song asks what discipline is actually accomplishing. People are neglected as individuals, organized into a mass, punished into obedience and made to look happy; yet nobody seems able to answer basic questions about what should happen next. The final car scene gives that failure a simple shape: a driver who cannot see, passengers who cannot steer, and a slogan promising spontaneous freedom. Jack does not need to name a particular institution for the arrangement to be recognizable. The song keeps testing the claim that being tightly controlled is the same as being safely guided.
reading: Care versus control; cohesion's justification contradicted by incompetent guidance and coerced reassurance.

revisions.editorial-4-heart-talk: The opening verb can mean managing someone, bothering with them or taking responsibility for them. The following refusal of a heart-to-heart pushes it toward neglect: nobody will attend to this person as a person. Yet the song soon supplies plenty of control—rules, blows and public conformity. That is the distinction to hear. The person can be disciplined without being cared for. The accusation of attention-seeking then makes the unmet need for recognition sound like another fault requiring correction.
revisions.phrase-4-magician: The magician is the last person who might have made an impossible change seem possible. Sending him home removes even that spectacle of rescue. What remains is assigned the respectable name 'discipline.' The line does not identify a hidden historical figure; its dramatic function is to shut down the hope raised by 'miracles.' In this sequence, discipline is what you are told to accept once no one intends to offer understanding or transformation. The circular refrain makes the naming sound settled before the experience has been justified.
revisions.discipline-loose-sand: This is the strongest argument the song allows the system to make: without organization, individuals will not hold together. The next lines test the means by which that cohesion is produced—beating, then scolding, then a life inside rules. Later, the group is united in the back seat of a badly driven car. They have indeed ceased to be scattered grains, but sharing a destination does not mean anyone knows how to reach it. The criticism is sharper than 'all rules are bad': organization can demand obedience without delivering competence or care.
revisions.discipline-fuel: The two questions are almost embarrassingly practical: are thieves going to be caught, and is the vehicle going to be refueled? They cut through the grand language of systems and discipline. Someone can keep talking and make everyone obey while failing at the elementary tasks that would justify their authority. The familiar encouragement contained in 'add fuel' adds another sting: telling people to keep going does not supply the means to go. The trembling legs and blind driver turn that gap between instructions and capability into a bodily danger.
revisions.editorial-4-blind-driver: The decisive pronoun is 'we.' The speaker is now inside the arrangement he has described, riding with everyone else instead of observing the crowd from outside. The driver controls the movement without being able to see; the passengers can see the problem without controlling the movement. This divides knowledge from power in an immediately understandable way. The travel slogan that follows calls the ride freedom, but its occupants have neither chosen the driver nor taken the wheel. Reassurance cannot repair that division.
